summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive platform that helps mission planners, researchers, educators, and the public evaluate potential lunar landing sites, particularly around the Moon’s south pole.

It combines 2D/3D terrain visualization, Sun and Earth visibility analysis, and side-by-side comparison of landing locations and dates to assess illumination, communication windows, and terrain conditions.

Our key differentiator is the integration of Citizen Science and the Lunar Grid Reference System (LGRS). Users can annotate high-resolution lunar imagery, identify potential surface hazards, and label illumination and shadow features, generating structured, georeferenced datasets that can support future scientific research and AI model training.

By using LGRS as a common spatial reference, we can organize, compare, and analyze neighboring regions consistently.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive platform for exploring, analyzing, and comparing potential lunar landing sites, particularly around the Moon’s south pole.

Missions targeting this region face significant challenges due to extreme variations in solar illumination, complex terrain, and limited direct-to-Earth communication opportunities. Small changes in landing location or date can significantly impact mission feasibility.

Our application brings together interactive 2D lunar mapping, 3D terrain visualization, topographic data, and Sun/Earth visibility analysis. Users can explore potential landing locations, inspect terrain and horizon profiles, evaluate illumination and communication windows, and compare different locations and landing dates.

Our goal is to make complex lunar environmental data easier to understand, helping mission planners evaluate alternative scenarios and assess potential operational constraints.

Lunar Grid Reference System (LGRS)

A central component of the platform is the Lunar Grid Reference System (LGRS), NASA's hierarchical lunar coordinate system, inspired by Earth's Military Grid Reference System (MGRS).

It provides four main spatial resolution levels:

  • 25 km: Global base grids using Lunar Transverse Mercator (LTM) and Lunar Polar Stereographic (LPS) projections.
  • 1 km: Regional subdivisions.
  • 100 m: Detailed local navigation.
  • 10 m: Condensed coordinates (ACC) for precise positioning.

Full LGRS coordinates can provide even finer precision, down to 1-meter cells.

This hierarchical structure provides a consistent spatial reference for navigating lunar regions and organizing geospatial information across different scales.

Citizen Science: Building a Lunar Geospatial Knowledge Base

One of our main differentiators is the integration of Citizen Science to generate structured, human-labelled lunar datasets.

Users can inspect high-resolution orbital imagery and contribute georeferenced annotations identifying surface hazards (boulders, craters, and obstacles), illumination and shadow boundaries, and potentially suitable landing areas.

Each observation can be associated with a spatial location, LGRS cell, image source, acquisition date, observation timestamp, category, and confidence level.

Our long-term vision is to organize these contributions into a spatio-temporal knowledge graph connecting locations, terrain features, imagery, observations, and environmental conditions.

This could create reusable datasets for training and evaluating future computer vision and machine learning models, with applications including lunar object detection, hazard identification, terrain classification, shadow segmentation, and change detection.

Community observations would undergo quality assessment and expert validation before being considered scientific ground truth.

Inspiration: NASA's MoonDiff Initiative

Our approach is inspired by NASA's MoonDiff initiative, which demonstrates how citizen scientists can identify lunar surface changes by comparing historical Lunar Orbiter imagery with more recent Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images. Their annotations are subsequently reviewed by lunar experts.

We aim to extend this participatory approach from identifying temporal changes to systematically characterizing lunar landing environments. By organizing observations through LGRS, our platform could make community-generated knowledge easier to compare, retrieve, validate, and reuse.

Future Development and Intended Impact

We envision a color-coded landing suitability layer combining terrain characteristics, potential hazards, solar illumination, and Earth visibility to provide an intuitive overview of favorable and unfavorable landing areas.

Although time constraints prevented its implementation, it remains part of our development roadmap, alongside more advanced scenario comparisons and temporal visualizations.

Ultimately, our goal is to bridge lunar mission planning, scientific visualization, and collaborative research. While providing an accessible tool for evaluating potential landing sites, we also aim to establish the foundations of a collaborative Lunar Geospatial Knowledge Base that could support future lunar missions and AI-assisted planetary exploration.

Technologies and Data

Technologies: React, TypeScript, Three.js, Python, FastAPI, Memgraph

Data sources: NASA LOLA topographic datasets, LROC imagery, LGRS datasets, and astronomical positioning data.

The platform integrates these sources into a unified environment for exploring lunar terrain, spatial references, and astronomical conditions.
dataRefs: GeoTIFF used to precalculate elevation angles for south pole sites
